title: The chief end (Westminster Shorter Catechism, 1647)
hookLine: Q1: our chief end is to glorify God and enjoy him forever

lines: WHAT IS THE CHIEF END OF MAN?
cards: A question, written for teaching: "What is the chief end of man?" Chief end. The main thing a human life is for.
You might expect a long answer: duty, rules, a list of obligations. The answer is one sentence: "Man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever."

It opens the Westminster Shorter Catechism, a little book of questions that Presbyterian and other Reformed churches use to teach the faith. This path met that sentence once before, in passing. Today it gets a whole day.

teach.b: Start with the word end. Here it doesn't mean the finish line. It means purpose, the thing something is for, the way a key is for opening a door.
So the question is: what is a person for? Now look at the grammar.
Glorify, and enjoy: two verbs, but one end, singular. The catechism doesn't give a life a serious purpose and, separately, a pleasant one.
It joins them with a single and: giving God glory and delighting in God are one thing. Then two words at the close: for ever. Not only on good days.
That's where the sentence meets these last weeks of hard questions. The catechism backs its answers with scripture, and one passage given here is Psalm seventy-three.

After one line on God's goodness, it turns to a man who nearly gave up: "my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped." He watched cruel people do well and good people suffer, and it was "too painful for me."
Until he went into the sanctuary of God. Then: "Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee."
And, still honest: "My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever." His body failing, his heart failing, and still, enjoyment of God.

teach.h: EAT, OR DRINK: TO THE GLORY OF GOD.
teach.b: Paul brings the same end down to the kitchen table: "whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." A whole teaching about God, and its first answer has the word enjoy in it.

how: In Presbyterian and other Reformed churches, children and new members can learn the Westminster Shorter Catechism by question and answer, starting from this first question.

s: in the catechism, end means the end of your life
it means purpose: what a person is for.
the answer gives a life two separate ends, one serious and one pleasant
it names one end, with two verbs joined by a single and: to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever.
in Psalm 73, the singer nearly gives up before he calls God his portion
"my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped." only later does he say God is his portion for ever.

games.q: you're the singer of Psalm 73. you've watched cruel people do well and good people suffer, and it's too painful to understand. what do you do?
o: go into the sanctuary of God.
quit, and decide it was all for nothing.
go and argue it out with the cruel people.
games.why: he goes into the sanctuary of God, and ends up saying: "whom have I in heaven but thee?" the joy comes after the slipping, not instead of it.

practice: Choose one small thing within reach, the warmth of a cup, light on a wall, the taste of what you last ate, a sound from the next room, and stay with it, without analyzing, until it is simply good to you.
If you pray, let that enjoyment be your thanks, without adding words; if you don't, let the small thing be enough for now.
